::: {.hero}
# Weather & TTC Delays
A JSC370 final project by Xiran Yin — exploring how 12 years of Toronto weather data predict subway delays using inferential statistics and machine learning.
:::

## Project Overview

The Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) carries over **one million daily riders**, making subway reliability a critical piece of urban infrastructure. This project asks a simple but practical question: **can daily weather conditions predict how badly the subway will be delayed?** And if so, **which weather features matter most**?

Using **roughly 4,400 daily observations from 2014–2025**, this project integrates two independent data sources — historical weather records and the City of Toronto's complete public record of TTC subway delays — to:

1. **Quantify** the statistical relationship between weather and total daily delay duration through OLS regression and Generalized Additive Models (GAM).
2. **Predict** delay severity using three supervised machine learning models (Linear/Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost), evaluated under both regression and classification framings on a chronologically held-out 2024–2025 test set.

## Key Findings

::: {.card-container}

::: {.card}
### Weather matters — but non-linearly
Snowfall has roughly **10× the per-unit delay impact** of liquid precipitation. The precipitation–delay relationship plateaus near 10 mm/day, and temperature effects are **U-shaped** — delays rise at both freezing and extreme heat.
:::

::: {.card}
### XGBoost wins
Among three machine learning models, **XGBoost achieves the best out-of-sample performance** for both regression (continuous total delay) and classification (top-quartile severe delay days). Random Forest is a close second; linear models lag substantially.
:::

::: {.card}
### Top predictors
Feature importance analysis ranks **snowfall**, **mean temperature**, and **day-of-week** as the strongest predictors of severe delay days — consistent with both the GAM smooths and the OLS coefficient signs.
:::

::: {.card}
### Convergent evidence
The same three features that explain the most variance in OLS and GAM also carry the most weight in XGBoost — convergence across linear, spline-based, and tree-based model classes.
:::

:::

## Data Sources

| Source | Coverage | Access |
|:-------|:---------|:-------|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Toronto daily weather, 2014-01-01 to 2026-01-01 | Free public API |
| [Toronto Open Data — TTC Subway Delays](https://open.toronto.ca/dataset/ttc-subway-delay-data/) | Every recorded subway delay 2014–2025 | CKAN API |

## Reproducibility

The full project is reproducible from a single command. Clone the repository and run:

```bash
quarto render
```

This will re-fetch the weather and TTC data from their public APIs, fit all models, and rebuild the website. See the [README](https://github.com/xiran-yin/JSC370-finalproject/blob/main/README.md) for setup instructions.
